# Kyde

> Kyde is behavioral scoring for AI agents. Every action an agent takes crosses Kyde and is scored against that agent's own normal behavior; the score sets what the agent may do, and an agent that drifts, is hijacked by prompt injection or gets stuck in a loop that burns money is stopped and handed to a human. Underneath is a control layer that checks identity, policy, data and limits at the moment of action and keeps a tamper-evident record an auditor can recompute. Any model, any vendor, on-prem, built in Europe. On top of that layer, Kyde also builds AI workers out of the processes a company already runs.

## The problem

AI agents don't fail loudly. They fail expensively. An agent is checked once, on the day it goes live; after that, the only one watching it is the agent itself. Three things go wrong, and each is usually found weeks later, from a customer, a bill or an auditor:

- **Loops (money).** An agent retries, loops and calls tools again and again overnight. Tokens, compute and API costs pile up; the invoice is the first alert.
- **Hijack (security).** A document, website, email or tool response carries instructions (prompt injection). The agent follows them with the operator's credentials, for example exporting customer data to an outside address.
- **Drift (behavior).** The agent stops behaving like itself: a vendor swaps the model, context and memory grow, the environment changes. Example: after a model update, a claims agent that normally approves six claims in ten approves every claim.

## How Kyde works

Behavioral scoring, the way banks score card payments: a card gets a score once when you apply, then the bank scores how you use it, the score sets your limit, and unusual use blocks the card. Kyde does the same for agents. Every agent gets a limit.

1. **Observe.** Every action of an agent crosses Kyde, through a gateway or SDK. No changes to the agent's logic.
2. **Learn.** Kyde learns each agent's normal behavior (a frozen baseline). Every human decision sharpens it.
3. **Score.** Every run is scored against the agent's own normal behavior. Deterministic statistics, recomputable from the record; no LLM judge in the detection path.
4. **Limit.** The score decides what the agent may do.
5. **Stop.** A drifting, hijacked or looping agent goes into quarantine; a human decides what happens next.
6. **Prove** (under every step). A tamper-evident, hash-chained record of everything; every score can be recomputed by a third party.

Detection runs two channels against the same frozen baseline: a divergence channel for gradual drift (behavior wandering over weeks) and a change-point channel (CUSUM family) for abrupt change after an input or update. Measured on public records, each catches events the other misses.

Any model, any vendor, on-prem, built in Europe. Runs in the customer's network; data stays with the customer.

## Research behind the detection

Kyde publishes its research on behavioral drift: "Behavioral Drift in Autonomous LLM-driven Systems: A Survey of Detection Approaches and the Case for Deterministic Detection" (J. Eckel, J. Radehaus, v0.4, 2026-09-17), with reference detector code at https://github.com/kydehq/behavioral-drift-detection and a summary at https://kyde.com/behavioral-drift.

- "Behavioral drift" covers at least seven phenomena with different causes and detection cost: goal drift, context decay, reward hacking, deception, multi-agent drift, persistent drift (memory or self-modification), version drift (vendor model changes). Prompt injection is a cause that produces three of them.
- The detection core has to be deterministic: an LLM judge is itself an agent subject to the drift it is asked to measure, and its verdicts cannot be replayed. Statistics over an append-only boundary record can be recomputed by anyone.
- First measurements on six public corpora (boundary call records only: tool name, hashed parameters, status, attribution; no content): a silent model change is detected in 80–100% of trials once it visibly shifts the tool-call distribution (JSD ≥ 0.02), 0% on a same-version control; false-alarm rates vary so much between deployments that they must be calibrated per deployment; successful in-session prompt injections and reward hacking are nearly invisible to distribution-level statistics (they use the same tools as legitimate work), which is why sequence-level, per-task models are the next step.

The research is honest about limits: what does not cross the boundary (intent in a reasoning trace, a poisoned memory entry, deception with harmless surface text) is invisible to any detector built on boundary records.

## Kyde Gateway

**Kyde Gateway** is the model-agnostic governance proxy that implements the layer. It is OpenAI-compatible and drop-in: it intercepts every inference call, verifies agent identity, enforces behavioral scope, blocks out-of-policy actions before they execute, and writes every entry into a hash-chained ledger.

Every entry captures: who acted (agent identity + role), what happened (prompt, tool calls, response), why it decided (causal context: retrieval and reasoning chain), when (millisecond-precise timestamp), and the hash-chain link that makes tampering detectable.

Two editions, the same compose files, switched by one env-file setting:
- **Starter** — the public images from the open GitHub repository (github.com/kydehq/gateway): hash-chained but unsigned ledger, observe-only DLP.
- **Enterprise** — adds Ed25519/TPM audit signing (hardware-rootable via PKCS#11 / HSM) and inline enforcement, plus unlimited retention, agent identity enforcement, MCP per-tool policy, RBAC and air-gapped operation.

## Kyde AI Workers (paused)

Kyde also builds AI workers from the processes a company already runs, starting with an audit of one process area. The build service is paused until late October 2026; the platform is the focus.

## Deployment

Three modes, all requiring zero code changes to agent logic:
- **Environment variable**: `export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://gateway.kyde.com/v1`
- **Group Policy (GPO)**: enterprise fleet deployment, no developer action required
- **Hosted proxy**: managed, EU data residency

On-premise, private cloud or EU-hosted. Target latency overhead: under 100ms. The record leaves the customer's building only when they send it.

## Provider compatibility

OpenAI (GPT-4o, o1, o3), Anthropic (Claude Sonnet, Opus, Haiku), Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Ollama, local models via LMStudio/vLLM, MCP routing. Workers can run on open models, private models or a system the company already uses.

## Regulatory context

Kyde is **built for** these regimes — a product cannot make an organization compliant, since that depends on the deployment.

**EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689)**
High-Risk AI system enforcement deadline for Annex III (employment, credit, insurance, education, critical infrastructure, essential services): **December 2, 2027** (Digital Omnibus agreement, May 2026). Annex I embedded AI products: August 2028.

Key obligations for enterprises deploying AI agents:
- Article 12: Automatic logging throughout system lifecycle, tamper-evident, minimum 6-month retention
- Article 14: Human oversight capability — requires causal context capture, not just I/O logs
- Article 26: Deployer obligations — the enterprise bears compliance responsibility, not the LLM provider
- Article 49: Registration in EU database before deployment

Vendor-native logs (OpenAI, Anthropic consoles) do not satisfy Article 26's independence requirement. Kyde's out-of-band ledger is architecturally independent of the providers it logs.

**DORA (EU Regulation 2022/2554)**
In force since January 2025. Applies to financial entities. Article 30 requires ICT-related incident logs, up to two-year retention, independent of ICT third-party providers. Kyde's provider-independent ledger directly addresses this requirement.

**NIS-2**
Makes management personally liable for security controls, which is the buy reason in most conversations today.

**GDPR Articles 22 / 35**
Automated decision-making requirements and DPIA obligations apply to AI agent deployments in HR, credit, insurance and healthcare. Causal context capture supports Article 22 explainability requirements. Personal data captured during an audit is removed locally, before anything is stored.

**KI-MIG**
The German AI market surveillance act, in force since 29 July 2026: BaFin supervises AI used in regulated financial activity.

**UK DRCF (CMA, FCA, ICO, Ofcom)**
Joint foresight paper on agentic AI: organizational accountability is unchanged regardless of agent autonomy. "My agent did it" is not a defense.

**NIST AI RMF and SP 800-207**
SP 800-207 defines zero trust architecture for users and devices; agents inherit the principles but are not its subject. NIST's AI work converges on the same requirements: traceable identity, causal context capture, tamper-evident records in a layer independent of the systems it governs.

## Target verticals (EU AI Act Annex III)

- Banking and finance (credit scoring, risk assessment)
- Insurance (risk classification, claims, pricing)
- Healthcare administration (essential services)
- Critical infrastructure (energy, transport, water) — see Kyde Labs
- HR technology / recruiting (employment decisions)
- Public sector, manufacturing
- Education technology (assessment, admission)

## Key differentiator vs. adjacent solutions

- **vs. AI security tools (Zenity, Lakera, Prompt Security)**: Those are semantic firewalls — they inspect inputs and outputs for adversarial content. Kyde enforces behavioral policy, provides agent identity, and produces audit-grade records. Analogous to: antivirus vs. corporate law.
- **vs. observability tools (LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize)**: Those require framework-specific instrumentation and produce developer debug output. Kyde is framework-agnostic, out-of-band, and produces regulator-ready records with enforcement capability.
- **vs. platform-native governance (Microsoft Copilot Studio, AWS Bedrock Guardrails)**: Those govern within a single vendor's stack. Kyde governs the chain across all providers and platforms — the gap every hyperscaler leaves open because they cannot govern their competitors' infrastructure.
- **vs. agent platforms and automation consultancies**: Those build the worker and leave the control layer to somebody else. Kyde builds both, so there is no agent platform and security product to make meet in the middle.

What happened, what the score saw, what Kyde did. Plus the insurer's view: a behavioral score you can underwrite, like a telematics box in a car.

### Complete guides (topic clusters)

- [Behavioral Drift in AI Agents](https://kyde.com/behavioral-drift): Behavioral drift is not a single, well-defined phenomenon. At least seven related ways agent behavior can change, presented as Kyde's synthesis of the literature rather than an established taxonomy: drift can be inherited between agents, agents can stop before the work is done, reward hacking is related but different, and evaluations only show behavior under evaluation conditions. Which signals are measurable from production logs and at what cost, and the four gaps the research has not closed. 17 linked arXiv sources.
- [Zero Trust for AI Agents](https://kyde.com/zero-trust-for-ai-agents): Never trust, always verify, per action. The six verification dimensions (who, what, when, where, why, how), where existing frameworks stop, and how boundary enforcement works. FAQ.
- [EU AI Act Compliance for AI Agents](https://kyde.com/eu-ai-act-compliance): Annex III classification, Articles 12/14/26/49 obligations, December 2027 deadline, three structural compliance gaps, six-step action plan, FAQ.
- [AI Agent Governance: The Complete Enterprise Guide](https://kyde.com/ai-agent-governance): What governance is, why existing approaches fail, the four requirements (identity, scope, enforcement, ledger), regulatory context, architecture, vendor landscape, FAQ.
- [Shadow AI: What It Is, Why It's a Risk, and How to Stop It](https://kyde.com/shadow-ai): Entry vectors, security/compliance/liability implications, EU AI Act exposure, detection methods, governance-without-blocking approach, FAQ.
- [Qualified Electronic Ledger (eIDAS)](https://kyde.com/qualified-electronic-ledger): What eIDAS 2.0 and the qualified electronic ledger regime require, the REQ-7.5 key-storage benchmark, and how a boundary-written hash chain maps onto it.
- [AI Agent Insurance: Liability, Coverage, and the Evidence Infrastructure](https://kyde.com/ai-agent-insurance): Legal liability framework (EU AI Act, PLD 2024, DORA), coverage landscape (AIUC-1, Munich Re aiSure, HSB), why certification alone isn't enough, the four evidence requirements (complete, continuous, independent, tamper-evident), how KYDE enables insurability, FAQ.

### Named comparisons

Honest, dated vendor comparisons: two genuine strengths of the competitor, a side-by-side table, and where the architectures actually differ.

- [Kyde vs WitnessAI](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-witnessai): Employee AI usage security (probabilistic inference) vs autonomous agent governance (deterministic enforcement at the boundary).
- [Kyde vs Alinia AI](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-alinia): SDK-wrapped compliance guardrails vs a network boundary that covers agents nobody instrumented.
- [Kyde vs Geordie AI](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-geordie): Context engineering that steers agent behavior vs a deterministic boundary outside the agent's reach.
- [Kyde vs Kyvvu](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-kyvvu): In-process security kernel (SDK) vs an external gateway no agent can opt out of.
- [Kyde vs Lakera](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-lakera): Real-time prompt/agent/MCP threat detection (Check Point) vs deterministic policy enforcement with a hash-chained ledger.
- [Kyde vs Microsoft Agent 365](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-microsoft-agent-365): Opt-in Microsoft-native control plane vs a vendor-independent boundary covering agents that never registered.
- [Kyde vs Zenity](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-zenity): Estate-by-estate platform connectors (SaaS, cloud, device) vs one unavoidable network boundary with deterministic policy and a hash-chained ledger.
- [Kyde vs Noma Security](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-noma-security): AI security lifecycle platform (posture to runtime threat protection) vs deterministic agent mandates with tamper-evident boundary evidence.
- [Kyde vs Vanta](https://kyde.com/compare/kyde-vs-vanta): Program-level compliance automation (GRC) vs runtime enforcement and action-level evidence; positioned as a stack, not a choice.

## Company

Kyde builds the zero trust layer for AI, and the AI workers that run on it. Early stage, engineered in Germany, working with design partners in finance, insurance, healthcare, the public sector, critical infrastructure and manufacturing.

Website: https://kyde.com — Contact: hello@kyde.com

Category: **behavioral scoring for AI agents**. Naming: **Kyde** in running text, **KYDE** as the wordmark. The platform is *Kyde* (behavioral scoring for AI agents; the underlying control layer was previously called Kyde Zero Trust); the gateway that implements it is the *Kyde Gateway*; the build service, paused until late October 2026, is *Kyde AI Workers*. "Behavioral firewall" names the enforcement layer in the articles, not the company.
